content: Gordy Ainsleigh is recognized as a pioneer in the sport of ultradistance trail running. In 1974, he became the first individual to complete the Western States Endurance Run course on foot. At the time, this 100-mile (160 km) mountain trail, stretching from Squaw Valley Ski Resort to Auburn, California, was exclusively used for the 24-hour Tevis Cup equestrian race. When his horse became lame prior to the event, Ainsleigh chose to run the grueling course rather than seek another horse. He successfully completed the race in 23 hours and 47 minutes, marking the inception of the Western States Endurance Run and the modern sport of trail ultramarathons. During his youth and early adulthood, Ainsleigh worked in various physically demanding jobs, including as a woodcutter, logger, construction worker, and juvenile counselor, while pursuing his education. He attended Sierra College in Rocklin, California, as well as the University of California campuses in Santa Barbara and Davis. His athletic pursuits included track (specializing in the two-mile event) at Colfax High School, cross-country running, wrestling, and sailing at Sierra College, and wrestling at UC Santa Barbara. In 1983, he earned a Doctor of Chiropractic degree from Western States Chiropractic College in Portland, Oregon, and became licensed to practice in both California and Oregon. In the late 1980s, during years when he did not participate in the Western States 100, Ainsleigh volunteered his chiropractic expertise at the Michigan Bluff medical checkpoint to assist runners. Over time, he organized a team of chiropractors who collaborated with medical doctors and podiatrists to support athletes in safely completing the race. As a prominent figure in trail ultrarunning, Ainsleigh has completed the Western States 100 a total of 22 times, with his fastest finish recorded at 20 hours and 55 minutes in 1984. The sport of trail ultramarathons has since grown in popularity, attracting dedicated endurance athletes to some of the most scenic landscapes in North America and beyond. Ainsleigh also briefly held the record for the fastest marathon run by an individual weighing over 200 pounds, completing the Avenue of the Giants Marathon in May 1973 in 2 hours, 52 minutes, and 7 seconds. This race took place along the Eel River in Northern California, amidst the iconic giant sequoias. His friend, Ken Cowman Shirk, later surpassed this record at the same event two years later. In 1988, Ainsleigh began rock climbing with Dr. Zane Kime, a physician and researcher in alternative medicine who studied the health benefits of natural sunlight exposure. Through this collaboration, Ainsleigh became involved in Kime's scientific work and, in 1993, authored a medical journal article highlighting the significant role of sun exposure in preventing internal cancers. Additionally, he wrote an article on the life of Wendell Robie, the founder of the Western States Trail Ride and the modern sport of endurance riding, as well as Robie's legendary endurance horse. This story was published in the January 1978 issue of Western Horseman.
